title: The Living World
description: Grade 11 Biology: characteristics of living organisms, biodiversity and the need for classification, binomial nomenclature, and the taxonomic hierarchy. Notes, examples and a test.

topics.title: What Is 'Living'? Characteristics of Living Organisms
topics.concept:
Biology is the science of life. But what exactly does it mean to be living? Defining life is not as simple as it seems — a virus, a seed and a hibernating animal all challenge a quick definition. Instead, biologists describe a set of characteristic features that living organisms show. The two defining properties are metabolism and the ability to respond and self-organise; the others are important but not unique to life.

  • Growth — living things increase in mass and number of cells. In living organisms growth is from inside (intrinsic), unlike a non-living mountain or crystal which grows by addition from outside. Note that growth alone is not a defining feature, since dead cells can still swell with water.
  • Reproduction — producing offspring with features similar to the parents. Yet some organisms (e.g. sterile worker bees, mules) do not reproduce, so reproduction too is not an all-defining feature.
  • Metabolism — the sum of all chemical reactions occurring in the body. All living organisms show metabolism, and no non-living object does. This makes metabolism a defining feature of life. Metabolic reactions can even be carried out in a test tube, but such isolated reactions are not 'living' — life is a property of the organised whole.
  • Cellular organisation — all living organisms are made of one or more cells, the basic unit of life.
  • Consciousness / response to stimuli — the ability to sense the environment (light, heat, other organisms) and respond to it. This self-awareness of surroundings is considered the most important defining characteristic of living organisms.

So, living organisms are self-replicating, evolving, self-regulating interactive systems capable of responding to their environment. Properties like metabolism and consciousness are defining; growth and reproduction are characteristic but not exclusive to life.

examples.problem: Example 1: Why is metabolism considered a defining feature of life, while growth is not?
examples.solution:
A defining feature must be present in all living things and absent in all non-living things.

  • Metabolism (all the body's chemical reactions) occurs in every living organism and in no non-living object — so it is defining.
  • Growth occurs in non-living things too (e.g. a crystal or mountain growing by addition), so growth alone is not defining.
examples.answer: Because metabolism is found in all living organisms and never in non-living things, whereas growth also occurs in non-living objects, so it is not unique to life.

examples.problem: Example 2: Give one reason why reproduction cannot be the all-inclusive defining property of living organisms.
examples.solution:
Some living organisms do not reproduce.

  • Sterile worker bees and mules are alive but cannot reproduce.
  • So reproduction, though characteristic, is not shown by every living organism.
examples.answer: Because some living organisms (e.g. mules, sterile worker bees) do not reproduce, reproduction is not a universal defining property.

examples.problem: Example 3: How does growth in living organisms differ from growth in non-living objects?
examples.solution:
The source of growth is different.

  • In living organisms, growth occurs from within (intrinsic) by cell division and an increase in cell number/mass.
  • In non-living objects (e.g. a mountain), growth is by addition of material from outside.
examples.answer: Living organisms grow intrinsically (from inside, by cell division), whereas non-living objects grow by external addition of material.

recap:
• Life is described by characteristic features rather than a single simple definition.
  • Growth (intrinsic) and reproduction are characteristic but not exclusive to life.
  • Metabolism and consciousness (response to stimuli) are the defining features.
  • All living things are cellular; life is a property of the organised whole, not of isolated reactions.

quiz.q: Which of these is regarded as a DEFINING property of all living organisms?
quiz.explanation: Metabolism occurs in all living organisms and no non-living thing, making it a defining feature.

quiz.q: Growth in living organisms differs from that in non-living things because it is:
quiz.explanation: Living organisms grow intrinsically by cell division, unlike non-living objects which grow by external addition.

topics.title: Diversity and the Need for Classification
topics.concept:
There is an enormous diversity of living organisms on Earth — so far about 1.7–1.8 million species have been described, and many more remain unknown. The number and types of organisms present on Earth make up its biodiversity. To study this vast variety, biologists give each kind a name and arrange them into groups — this is classification.

If every organism were known only by local (common) names, there would be chaos: the same plant may have many names in different languages and regions, and the same common name may be used for different organisms. To bring order, scientists identify each organism and place it in a category.

The branch of biology that deals with classification — identification, naming and grouping organisms — is called taxonomy. The basis of classification has changed over time: from simple uses (food, shelter, medicine) to external features, and now to internal structure, cell organisation, development and evolutionary relationships. The study of the kinds and diversity of organisms and the evolutionary relationships among them is called systematics.

Classification is essential because it: makes the study of a huge variety of organisms easy and systematic; helps us understand how different groups are related; and forms the basis for the study of other biological sciences. Each distinct kind of organism that we classify is given the basic unit of classification — the species.

examples.solution:
Both deal with classifying organisms but differ slightly.

  • Taxonomy is the science of identification, naming and classification of organisms.
  • Systematics is the study of the diversity of organisms and their evolutionary relationships.
examples.answer: Taxonomy is the identification, naming and classification of organisms; systematics also studies their diversity and evolutionary relationships.

examples.problem: Example 2: Why are common (local) names of organisms unsuitable for scientific study?
examples.solution:
Common names are not standardised.

  • The same organism has different names in different languages/regions.
  • The same name may be used for different organisms, causing confusion worldwide.
examples.answer: Because common names vary by region and language and may refer to different organisms, causing confusion; a universal scientific name is needed.

examples.problem: Example 3: State two reasons why classification of organisms is necessary.
examples.solution:
Classification organises biodiversity.

  • It makes the study of a huge variety of organisms easy and systematic.
  • It reveals relationships among groups and is the basis for other biological studies.
examples.answer: It makes studying the vast diversity of life systematic and easy, and it shows how different groups are related.

recap:
• Earth has enormous biodiversity (~1.7–1.8 million species described).
  • Classification brings order; taxonomy = identification, naming, classification.
  • Systematics also studies diversity and evolutionary relationships.
  • Common names are unreliable; the basic unit of classification is the species.

quiz.q: The science of identification, naming and classification of organisms is:
quiz.explanation: Taxonomy deals with the identification, naming and classification of organisms.

quiz.q: The total number and variety of organisms on Earth is called:
quiz.explanation: Biodiversity is the number and types of organisms present on Earth.

topics.title: Nomenclature and Taxonomic Categories
topics.concept:
To give every organism a single, universally accepted scientific name, biologists use binomial nomenclature, a system given by Carolus Linnaeus. Each name has two parts: the genus (generic name) and the species (specific epithet) — for example, the mango is Mangifera indica and humans are Homo sapiens.

There are agreed rules for writing scientific names:

  • Names are usually in Latin and written in italics.
  • The first word (genus) begins with a capital letter; the second word (species) begins with a small letter.
  • When handwritten, both words are underlined separately to show they are Latin.
  • The name of the author who first described the species may be written after it (in abbreviated form), e.g. Mangifera indica Linn.

Organisms are arranged in a series of categories from the lowest to the highest — the taxonomic hierarchy. Each level is a taxon (plural: taxa). The categories, from lowest to highest, are: Species → Genus → Family → Order → Class → Phylum (or Division for plants) → Kingdom. As we go up, the number of common features decreases and the group becomes larger. The species is the basic unit — a group of individuals with fundamental similarities that can interbreed.

Biologists also use taxonomic aids to identify and study organisms, such as the herbarium (pressed, dried plant specimens), botanical gardens and zoological parks, museums, and identification keys.

examples.problem: Example 1: In the scientific name Mangifera indica, identify the genus and the species, and state who introduced binomial nomenclature.
examples.solution:
A binomial name has a genus and a species part.

  • Genus (generic name): Mangifera.
  • Species (specific epithet): indica.
  • Binomial nomenclature was given by Carolus Linnaeus.
examples.answer: Genus = Mangifera, species = indica; binomial nomenclature was introduced by Carolus Linnaeus.

examples.problem: Example 2: State any two rules for writing the scientific name of an organism.
examples.solution:
There are agreed conventions.

  • The genus starts with a capital letter and the species with a small letter.
  • Names are written in italics (or underlined separately when handwritten).
examples.answer: The genus begins with a capital and the species with a small letter; the name is italicised (or underlined separately by hand).

examples.problem: Example 3: Arrange these taxonomic categories from lowest to highest: Order, Species, Family, Kingdom, Genus.
examples.solution:
Recall the taxonomic hierarchy.

  • Species → Genus → Family → Order → ... → Kingdom.

recap:
• Binomial nomenclature (by Linnaeus) gives each organism a two-part Latin name: Genus + species, written in italics (genus capitalised, species small).
  • The taxonomic hierarchy: Species → Genus → Family → Order → Class → Phylum/Division → Kingdom; each level is a taxon.
  • Going up the hierarchy, common features decrease and group size increases; species is the basic unit.
  • Taxonomic aids: herbarium, botanical gardens, zoological parks, museums, keys.

quiz.q: The two-part naming system for organisms (e.g. Homo sapiens) was given by:
Which is the correct order of taxonomic categories from lowest to highest?
quiz.explanation: The hierarchy from lowest to highest is Species, Genus, Family, Order (then Class, Phylum, Kingdom).

questions.q: Which of the following is a defining feature of all living organisms?
questions.explanation: Metabolism is present in all living organisms and no non-living thing, so it is defining.

questions.q: Growth in living organisms is said to be intrinsic because it occurs:
questions.explanation: Living organisms grow from within by an increase in cell number and mass.

questions.q: Reproduction is NOT an all-defining feature of life because:
options: Some living organisms (e.g. mules) do not reproduce
questions.explanation: Sterile organisms like mules and worker bees are alive but do not reproduce.

questions.q: The most important defining property of living organisms is considered to be:
questions.explanation: The ability to sense and respond to the environment (consciousness) is the key defining feature.

questions.q: The number and types of organisms present on Earth is referred to as:
questions.explanation: Biodiversity is the variety and number of organisms on Earth.

questions.q: The science of identification, naming and classification of organisms is:
questions.explanation: Taxonomy deals with identification, naming and classification.

questions.q: The study of diversity of organisms and their evolutionary relationships is:
questions.explanation: Systematics studies diversity and evolutionary relationships among organisms.

questions.q: The two-part scientific naming system is called:
questions.explanation: Binomial nomenclature gives a two-part (genus + species) name.

questions.q: Binomial nomenclature was introduced by:
questions.explanation: Carolus Linnaeus gave the binomial system of nomenclature.

questions.q: In the name Mangifera indica, the word 'indica' is the:
questions.explanation: The second word is the specific epithet (species name).

questions.q: According to the rules, the genus name is written with:
questions.explanation: The genus begins with a capital letter; the species with a small letter.

questions.q: Each rank or level in the classification hierarchy is called a:
questions.explanation: Each level in the taxonomic hierarchy is a taxon.

questions.q: The basic unit of classification is the:
questions.explanation: The species is the basic unit of classification.

questions.q: The correct sequence of taxonomic categories from lowest to highest is:
options: Species, Genus, Family, Order, Class, Phylum, Kingdom
Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species
questions.explanation: From lowest to highest: Species, Genus, Family, Order, Class, Phylum/Division, Kingdom.

questions.q: A collection of pressed, dried and mounted plant specimens used as a taxonomic aid is a:
questions.explanation: A herbarium stores pressed, dried plant specimens for study.

questions.q: Metabolic reactions carried out in a test tube (outside the body) are 'living reactions' but the test tube is not living. This shows that life is a property of:
options: The organised whole, not isolated reactions
questions.explanation: Life emerges from the organised, interacting whole; isolated reactions in a tube are not 'living'.

questions.q: As we move up the taxonomic hierarchy from species to kingdom, the number of common characteristics:
questions.explanation: Higher categories are larger and share fewer common features than lower ones.

questions.q: Why must scientific names be in a standardised form (italics, capital genus, small species) worldwide?
options: So that one universal name avoids the confusion of varied local names
To make them harder to read
Because Latin is the only language
questions.explanation: A single standardised binomial name is understood by scientists everywhere, unlike varied common names.

questions.q: A mule cannot reproduce, yet it is undoubtedly living. This is best explained by saying that:
options: Reproduction is characteristic but not a universal defining feature
Reproduction is the only sign of life
questions.explanation: Some living organisms do not reproduce, so reproduction is not an all-defining property; metabolism is.

questions.q: Two organisms placed in the same FAMILY but different GENERA will share:
options: Fewer common features than two in the same genus
More common features than two in the same genus
questions.explanation: The lower the shared category, the more features in common; same-genus organisms share more than same-family ones.

questions.q: Which taxonomic aid would a botanist MOST likely use to compare a newly collected plant with previously identified, pressed specimens?
questions.explanation: A herbarium holds dried, mounted, identified plant specimens for comparison and reference.
